# Prompting LTX

Models: LTX-2.5. A good prompt runs about 1000 characters.

LTX reads a prompt as a shot description, not a caption. Write one flowing paragraph in the present tense, covering Lightricks' six elements in its documented order and dropping any the request does not need:

Establish the shot, then set the scene and lighting, then the action, then the characters, then the camera movement, then the audio.

**Establish the shot first.** Open with shot scale and setting in shot-list form: "Medium wide shot, exterior, narrow street at dusk." Use the standard sizes (extreme wide shot, wide shot, medium wide shot, medium shot, medium close-up, close-up, extreme close-up) and state the angle separately when it matters: a low-angle medium shot is a different instruction from a medium shot. A named style (painterly, film noir, analog film look, claymation, 8-bit pixel) belongs in this opening, because styles work best when named early.

**Length.** A single shot usually takes four to eight descriptive sentences. Match detail to shot scale: a close-up needs more precise detail than a wide shot.

**Action and characters.** Write the action as a natural sequence from beginning to end. Give characters age, hairstyle, clothing, and distinguishing details. Express feeling through the body: "his shoulders drop and his jaw tightens", not "he is sad". Put blocking in frame terms and in order: "she steps from the left third of frame into the centre, turning to face camera as she arrives."

**Camera.** Use Lightricks' own words, because a synonym is a worse prompt: follows, tracks, pans across, circles around, tilts upward, pushes in, pulls back, overhead view, handheld movement, over-the-shoulder, wide establishing shot, static frame. Write "static frame" for a locked camera: leaving the camera out is not the same instruction. Describe the move relative to the subject, keep to one move per shot, and say where it lands: "the camera tracks her from her left side at chest height; as the move settles, she sits centre frame with the shutter filling the background behind her." When the camera motion setting is chosen, it supplies the move, so write no other.

**Audio.** LTX generates sound with the picture. Describe ambience, music and speech plainly, and put every spoken line in quotation marks, naming the language and accent when it matters. A speaker label with a delivery note also works: Baker (whispering): "Today I achieve perfection."

**Several shots.** LTX-2.5 can cut inside one clip, but only when the request carries distinct shots. Keep to two to four, written as one chronological paragraph rather than a numbered list. At every cut, name the transition ("A hard cut transitions to a medium close-up of..."), re-establish shot size and angle, reuse the same identifying words for a recurring subject, and say whether the music or dialogue continues across the cut.

**With a start frame.** The image already fixes the subject, wardrobe, colours and composition, so the prompt describes what happens, not what it looks like, in one continuous take. With a start and an end frame, describe the path between them: "the heavy wooden door swings slowly open, warm light spilling across the stone floor. Hinges creak."

**Text.** Exact spelling across frames is not guaranteed. Keep any on-screen text short and prominent.

**Avoid.** Emotional labels without a visible cue. Fast, non-linear motion such as jumping, juggling or tumbling, which produces artifacts (dancing is fine). Crowded frames: the more characters and actions, the more of them go missing. Conflicting light sources, such as a warm sunset with a cold fluorescent glow, unless the scene motivates both. Two camera moves in one shot. Opening with a camera move before the subject exists.
